title: Rotational Dynamics
subject: Physics
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: Centripetal vs Centrifugal Force: Core distinction?
cards.a: Centripetal force is a real force directed towards the center (F = m v² / r = m ω² r). Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force experienced in a rotating (non-inertial) frame directed away from the center.
cards.hint: Centrifugal force is NOT the reaction to centripetal force; it exists only in rotating frames.

cards.q: Kinematical equations for uniform angular acceleration α?
cards.a:
1. ω = ω₀ + α t
2. θ = ω₀ t + (1/2) α t²
3. ω² = ω₀² + 2 α θ.
cards.hint: Analogous to linear equations: replace v → ω, u → ω₀, a → α, s → θ.

cards.q: Maximum safe speed of a vehicle on an unbanked circular road?
cards.a: v_max = √(μ_s r g), where μ_s is coefficient of static friction, r is radius of curve, and g is acceleration due to gravity.
cards.hint: Independent of the mass of the vehicle! Friction alone provides centripetal force.

cards.q: Optimum (banking) angle θ for a road without relying on friction?
cards.a: tan θ = v₀² / (r g) ⇒ v₀ = √(r g tan θ).
cards.hint: At this design speed v₀, there is zero wear and tear of tires and no frictional force is needed.

cards.q: Upper and lower speed limits on a banked road with friction?
cards.a:
v_max = √[ r g (tan θ + μ_s) / (1 - μ_s tan θ) ]
v_min = √[ r g (tan θ - μ_s) / (1 + μ_s tan θ) ].
cards.hint: If tan θ ≤ μ_s, v_min = 0 (vehicle can stand parked without slipping down).

cards.q: Time period and tension for a Conical Pendulum of length L and semi-vertical angle θ?
cards.a:
Time Period: T = 2π √(L cos θ / g) = 2π √(h / g)
Tension: T₀ = m g / cos θ.
cards.hint: h = L cos θ is the vertical height of the cone. T is smaller than that of a simple pendulum.

cards.q: Minimum speed in a Well of Death (Rotor) of radius r?
cards.a: v_min = √(r g / μ_s).
cards.hint: Normal reaction N provides centripetal force (N = m v² / r) and vertical friction balances weight (f_s = μ_s N = m g).

cards.q: Vertical Circular Motion: Critical speeds at Highest (H), Lowest (L), and Midway (M) points?
cards.a:
v_H = √(r g)
v_M = √(3 r g)
v_L = √(5 r g).
cards.hint: Speeds are derived assuming string just remains taut at highest point (tension T_H = 0).

cards.q: Difference in tension between Lowest and Highest points in Vertical Circular Motion?
cards.a: T_L - T_H = 6 m g.
cards.hint: Classic MHT-CET result! This difference is completely independent of initial velocity as long as the circle is completed.

cards.q: What is Moment of Inertia (MI) and Radius of Gyration (K)?
cards.a:
MI: I = ∑ m_i r_i² = ∫ r² dm (rotational analogue of mass; measures rotational inertia).
Radius of Gyration: K = √(I / M) (effective distance from axis where entire mass can be assumed concentrated).
cards.hint: SI unit of MI: kg·m² [M¹ L² T⁰]. K depends on mass distribution and axis location, NOT on total mass.

cards.q: State the Theorem of Parallel Axes.
cards.a: I_O = I_C + M h², where I_C is MI about an axis through center of mass, and h is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.
cards.hint: Crucial: One of the axes MUST strictly pass through the Center of Mass (I_C).

cards.q: State the Theorem of Perpendicular Axes.
cards.a: I_Z = I_X + I_Y, for a planar lamina in the X-Y plane, where Z-axis is perpendicular to the lamina.
cards.hint: Applies strictly to 2D planar bodies (discs, rings, plates), never to 3D solid bodies like spheres.

cards.q: Moment of Inertia of a Ring of mass M and radius R?
cards.a:
Transverse central axis: I = M R²
About diameter: I = (1/2) M R²
Tangential perpendicular to plane: I = 2 M R²
Tangential in plane: I = (3/2) M R².
cards.hint: Use perpendicular axis theorem for diameter: I_Z = I_X + I_Y ⇒ M R² = 2 I_d ⇒ I_d = (1/2) M R².

cards.q: Moment of Inertia of a Uniform Disc of mass M and radius R?
cards.a:
Transverse central axis: I = (1/2) M R²
About diameter: I = (1/4) M R²
Tangential perpendicular to plane: I = (3/2) M R²
Tangential in plane: I = (5/4) M R².
cards.hint: Disc MI is exactly half that of a ring about the corresponding central axis.

cards.q: Moment of Inertia of Solid Sphere vs Hollow Sphere (Spherical Shell)?
cards.a:
Solid Sphere: I_diameter = (2/5) M R², I_tangent = (7/5) M R²
Hollow Sphere: I_diameter = (2/3) M R², I_tangent = (5/3) M R².
cards.hint: Hollow sphere has higher MI than solid sphere of same mass and radius because mass is farther from axis.

cards.q: Moment of Inertia of a thin uniform rod of length L?
cards.a:
About central axis perpendicular to length: I = M L² / 12
About transverse axis through one end: I = M L² / 3.
cards.hint: By parallel axis theorem: I_end = M L² / 12 + M (L/2)² = M L² / 3.

cards.q: Relations between Torque, Angular Momentum, and Moment of Inertia?
cards.a:
Torque: τ = I α = dL / dt
Angular Momentum: L = I ω = r × p.
Rotational Kinetic Energy: K_rot = (1/2) I ω² = L² / (2 I).
cards.hint: Torque is rotational analogue of Force (F = m a); Angular Momentum is analogue of Linear Momentum (p = m v).

cards.q: State the Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum with real-life examples.
cards.a:
If external torque τ_ext = 0, then L = I ω = constant (i.e. I₁ ω₁ = I₂ ω₂).
Examples: Ballet dancer tucking in arms (I ↓ ⇒ ω ↑), diver somersaulting.
cards.hint: Decreasing moment of inertia automatically increases angular velocity to keep L conserved.

cards.q: Total Kinetic Energy of a body rolling without slipping?
cards.a: E = K_trans + K_rot = (1/2) M v² + (1/2) I ω² = (1/2) M v² [ 1 + K² / R² ], where K is radius of gyration.
cards.hint: Fraction of energy in translation: 1 / [1 + K²/R²]; in rotation: (K²/R²) / [1 + K²/R²].

cards.q: Velocity and acceleration of a rolling body down an inclined plane of height h and angle θ?
cards.a:
v = √[ 2 g h / (1 + K² / R²) ]
a = [ g sin θ ] / [ 1 + K² / R² ].
cards.hint: Bodies with smaller K²/R² reach bottom faster! Order of arrival: Solid Sphere > Disc > Hollow Sphere > Ring.

cards.q: Value of K² / R² for standard rolling bodies?
cards.a:
Ring / Hollow Cylinder: K² / R² = 1
Disc / Solid Cylinder: K² / R² = 1/2 = 0.5
Hollow Sphere: K² / R² = 2/3 ≈ 0.67
Solid Sphere: K² / R² = 2/5 = 0.4.
cards.hint: Solid sphere has the smallest K²/R² (0.4), so it rolls down fastest with highest acceleration!

cards.q: Condition for pure rolling (rolling without slipping)?
cards.a:
v_cm = R ω, and acceleration a_cm = R α.
At the point of contact with ground, instantaneous velocity is ZERO (v_contact = 0).
cards.hint: Work done by friction in pure rolling is zero because point of contact is instantaneously at rest.

cards.q: If Earth suddenly shrinks to half its radius without change in mass, what is the new duration of day?
cards.a:
T₂ = 6 hours.
Since I = (2/5) M R², shrinking to R/2 makes I₂ = I₁ / 4. By conservation of L: I₁ ω₁ = I₂ ω₂ ⇒ ω₂ = 4 ω₁ ⇒ T₂ = T₁ / 4 = 24 / 4 = 6 h.
cards.hint: Frequent Board & MHT-CET problem! T ∝ R² when mass is constant.

cards.q: Power delivered by torque and work done in rotational motion?
cards.a:
Work: W = ∫ τ dθ = τ · θ (for constant torque)
Power: P = dW / dt = τ · ω.
cards.hint: Direct rotational analogue of W = F · s and P = F · v.

cards.q: MHT-CET Trap: Can Radius of Gyration K be negative or zero for a real body?
cards.a: NO. K = √(I / M) is a geometric distance measure and is ALWAYS strictly POSITIVE (K > 0).
cards.hint: SI unit of K is metre (m); its dimensional formula is [M⁰ L¹ T⁰].
